meta.title: Who really said "I would rather die of passion than of boredom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not van Gogh's own words. The line is Émile Zola's, from his 1883 novel Au Bonheur des Dames; van Gogh merely quoted it, crediting Zola, in an 1884 letter.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I would rather die of passion than of boredom'?
meta.ogDescription: It's Émile Zola's line from Au Bonheur des Dames (1883). Van Gogh quoted it in an 1884 letter to Theo, crediting Zola — then it got pinned on him alone.

answer.label: Not Vincent van Gogh — actually Émile Zola
answer.authorDates: 1840–1902 · French novelist, quoted by Vincent van Gogh
answer.sourceLine: The line belongs to novelist Émile Zola: it is spoken by the character Octave Mouret in Zola’s 1883 novel Au Bonheur des Dames (“The Ladies’ Paradise”) — in French, “je préfère crever de passion que de crever d’ennui.” Van Gogh copied the passage into a letter to his brother Theo on 2 October 1884, openly crediting “Octave Mouret” and Zola. As Quote Investigator concludes, Zola should be credited — van Gogh was quoting, not coining.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: Au Bonheur des Dames (The Ladies’ Paradise)
“Crever pour crever, je préfère crever de passion que de crever d’ennui !” — spoken by Octave Mouret
Vincent van Gogh, letter to Theo, 2 October 1884

source.excerpt: Crever pour crever, je préfère crever de passion que de crever d’ennui ! — “Death against death, I would rather die of passion than of ennui!”
trail: Quote Investigator traces the saying to Émile Zola’s 1883 novel Au Bonheur des Dames, spoken by the character Octave Mouret.
Van Gogh quoted the passage — crediting “Octave Mouret” and Zola — in his letter to Theo of 2 October 1884.
An English rendering of the letter shows van Gogh introducing the extract with “from Octave Mouret” before the “die of passion…boredom” lines.
source.excerptNote: Zola’s original French and the 1883 English rendering. The popular “boredom” wording is a light modernization of “ennui.”

source.rightsNote: The words are Émile Zola’s, from Au Bonheur des Dames (1883); both the French original and the contemporaneous 1883 English translation are long in the public domain in the U.S. (first published well before 1931). The popular “boredom” phrasing is a modern paraphrase of the period translation’s “ennui.”

author.name: Émile Zola
author.heading: About Émile Zola
author.metaLine: 1840–1902 · French novelist, leader of literary Naturalism
author.bio: Émile Zola was the leading figure of French literary Naturalism, best known for his twenty-novel Les Rougon-Macquart cycle dissecting society under the Second Empire. Au Bonheur des Dames (1883), the eleventh novel, follows the rise of a Paris department store and its ambitious owner Octave Mouret, whose appetite for risk voices the “die of passion” credo. Van Gogh, an avid reader of Zola, absorbed and quoted him admiringly — which is how this line drifted onto the painter.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on van Gogh
misattribution.intro: Quote sites and image memes credit the line to Vincent van Gogh, because he wrote it in a famous letter. But he was quoting — and said so.

items.why: Van Gogh copied the passage into his 2 October 1884 letter to Theo and expressly attributed it to Zola’s character Octave Mouret. Aggregators such as Goodreads and Quotefancy drop that context and file it under van Gogh alone.

misattribution.truthLine: The originator is Émile Zola (1883); van Gogh was an admiring reader who quoted him, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line reads like a painter’s manifesto, which is why it fused so naturally to van Gogh. In truth it is a merchant’s creed: Zola gives it to Octave Mouret, the department-store magnate of Au Bonheur des Dames, as a defense of appetite and risk over cautious comfort.
Van Gogh, then defending his own turbulent choices to Theo, found in Mouret’s words a mirror for his temperament — and by transcribing them, unwittingly set them on the road to becoming ‘his.’
context.pull: Van Gogh didn’t coin it — he recognized himself in it.
